name: Mahmud Sami al-Barudi
bio: Mahmud Sami ibn Hasan Husni al-Barudi was born in Cairo in 1255 AH (1839 CE) to a family of Circassian descent; al-Zirikli traces the name to Itay al-Barud in Egypt, which one of his forebears had held as a tax farm. A graduate of the military school, he was among the commanders of the Egyptian forces sent to help the Ottomans in the Cretan revolt and in the Russian war of 1877, rose through office to head the cabinet in 1882, with Ahmad Urabi as his minister of war, and when the Urabi revolt failed he was sentenced to death, a sentence commuted to exile in Ceylon, the Arabs' Sarandib. He spent seventeen years there, most of them in Kandy, learned English and lost his sight, and was pardoned in 1317 AH (1899 CE) and came home. Al-Zirikli calls him “the first in our time to raise Arabic poetry from its fall”, and he is counted the pioneer of the revival school, al-Ihya' wa-l-Ba'th, known in English studies as neoclassicism; Shawqi Dayf, for whom he was “the first of the renewers of modern Arabic poetry” for bringing back the strength of the old style, counts him with Ahmad Shawqi and Hafiz Ibrahim among the poets of the revival and calls him Hafiz's ideal. He died in Cairo in 1322 AH (1904 CE).
